content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes "Multi-level contrastive learning" as a self-supervised approach to learning region-level representations of images. As is becoming standard in SSL, the approach applies a contrastive loss to features produced by an online network and a target network (that represents an exponential moving average of the online network). The key idea is to convert the input into each network into a multiscale image montage. Multiscale features are produced using a feature pyramid, and the positive and negative samples for the contrastive loss are determined programmatically at each scale during montage creation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*Strengths:*

(1) The proposed method outperforms many other recent works on SSL for dense computer vision tasks,

(2) The proposed method needs iterations of pretraining, and

(3) To my knowledge, using image montages as a pretext task for SSL is a new idea.

*Weaknesses:*

(1) I found the paper difficult to follow (specific concerns in the next box),

(2) The paper fails to compare to [1], which seems to achieve similar if not better results on COCO tasks under the same evaluation criteria,

(3) The ablation studies add little value to the paper (specific concerns in the next box), and

(4) I do not think the methods of this paper would transfer to applications outside of computer vision. So, while it is an application of representation learning, I do not think that it has much appeal to the representation learning community at large.
[1] "Self-supervised Learning with Local Contrastive Loss for Detection and Semantic Segmentation" https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04398
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
*Clarity:* I found the paper difficult to follow for the following reasons.

(1) A key part of the methodology appears to be the positional encoding block, but all discussion of that is relegated to the appendix. Thus, it was difficult to get a full understanding of the method without flipping back-and-forth between several pages.

(2) Seeing a qualitative visualization of the output of a network trained with the proposed method would greatly aid clarity.

(3) In the introduction, the authors claim that supervised pretraining can lead to performance that is equivalent to self-supervised pretraining, “[W]e extend our pretext task to supervised pre-training, which achieves similar performance with self-supervised pretraining. This result breaks the empirical conclusion that SSL methods outperform their supervised counterparts…” (p2). In the ablation studies, the authors claim to verify that, “unsupervised pre-training, serving as a strong regularization, guides the learning towards basis of attraction of minima that support better generalization from the training data set.” (p9) These two conclusions seem at odds to me.

(4) In the Montage Downsampling Level ablation study, it states that, “Tab 8a is the result of MoCo v3 pre-trained by 100 epochs on COCO 2017 val set.” (p8) The caption for Table 8 states that, “All models are trained on ImageNet dataset for 100 epochs.” Which one is it?

(5) I cannot work out the settings for the experiments that generated Tables 1, 2, and 3 from the text or the captions. Sometimes the pretraining set is mentioned, other times it is not.

(6) There are numerous typos that need to be fixed.

*Quality:* The quality of the work is mixed. 

On the one hand: There is a clear comparison on standard benchmarks in the field. The method is intuitive and relatively easy to understand.

On the other hand: The ablation studies offer few meaningful insights. The conclusion of the ablation study on Montage Downsampling Level is, "[T]he representation of fine-grained objects is important for the COCO object detection dataset, in which 41% of objects are small." (p8) While the conclusion of the ablation study on Multi-Level Contrastive Loss is "[T]he representation from the low-resolution image is inferior to the high-resolution image." (p8) I struggle to see how these are materially different conclusions. Moreover, the fact that "41% of objects are small" is surely enough to draw this conclusion on its own, but the benefits of multi-scale (in particular, high-resolution) features have already appeared in many works, including [2] and [3].

The conclusion drawn from that the ablation study on Weight Decay, “supports the conclusion of (Erhan et al. 2010) that unsupervised pre-training, serv[es] as strong regularization,” (p9) is not obvious to me. The ablation study showed that “large weight decay leads to a superior result,” (p8) by varying the weight decay in the self-supervised pretraining. To support the claim that “unsupervised pre-training serv[es] as strong regularization,” wouldn’t the study need to compare unsupervised pre-training with supervised pretraining? What does weight decay have to do with this?

Finally, the conclusion of the ablation study on Training Epochs is, “[T]hat a long training schedule further improves the performance.” (p9) Again, this seems to be a fact of life in machine learning that needs no additional verification.

*Novelty:* I believe using image montages to generate a pretext task for dense SSL is novel. The rest of the set-up is standard in the dense SSL literature.

*Reproducibility:* I believe someone practiced in the art could produce similar results from a careful reading of the paper.

[2] "Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition" https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.03385v1.pdf

[3] "Deep High-Resolution Representation Learning for Visual Recognition" https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.07919.pdf
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend rejecting the paper. The primary innovation (image montages as inputs) seems like it could be of interest to the computer vision community in general, but I don’t see it being particularly useful to the representation learning community. As outlined above, the ablation studies offered little new insight into representation learning in general or this method specifically. As such, the value of the paper is limited to researchers in SSL methods for dense computer vision tasks. My recommendation is that the authors update the ablation studies, do another sweep through the existing literature on this topic, and resubmit to a computer vision conference, where this will likely be of more interest.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper mainly introduces a new method for image self-supervise learning that considers scale-invariant features. To this end, the paper proposes to assemble multi-scale images in a montage manner, which combines images of different downsampling ratios. In doing so, the feature of different levels is well-aligned.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: The idea of this paper is reasonable and makes sense to me. 
Weakness: Although the proposed method is effective, the reason behind it is not clearly stated. Is this caused by the specific design or inter-layers (FPN) contrastive loss? To make a fair comparison, the author should conduct experiments with other contrastive-based methods (for example, Dense CL) in the FPN architecture.
In addition, I think the method works because ImageNet is object-centric, which makes it reasonable to do such image-level rescaling and contrastive learning. Will this montage-based method still work with other pretraining benchmarks? As the selective-based method fails to achieve good performance because of the poor quality of the bounding boxes, I think the performance of the method with pretraining on non-object-centric is still unsatisfactory. This should be supported by extra experiments. 
In addition, the reason that causes faster convergence is not clear (inter-layer contrastive? or efficient data usage).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new self-supervised method for dense prediction tasks. The key idea is to design a new pretext task which constructs a montage image to mimic multi-scale and multi-object scenarios. After obtaining feature representations from the online network (student) and target network (target), a multi-level contrastive loss is further applied. The proposed method is evaluated on commonly used benchmarks and shows performance improvement.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea of constructing montage images is novel, even though its limitations are not clear enough (discussed in weakness).
2. The performance is good in some downstream tasks. 

Weakness:
1. In Equation 1, the target network is only appended with a projector. What’s the reason behind this? Is it reasonable to do contrastive loss between $u$ and $v$ where $u$ contains an extra predictor?
2. In Equation 1, what does the subscript $si$ mean? 
3. The idea of constructing a montage image has several limitations: (1) it cannot be applied to models with global attention, otherwise the features from subimage are not pure; (2) subimages should be simple enough. Ideally, each sub-image only contains one object; (3) will the features at the boundary of two subimages be problematic? and (4) Can we simply use something like [1] to generate multi-scale features then do some cross-scale contrastive loss [2]?     
4. As shown in Table 3, the performance improvement is marginal compared to SoCo. All of these baselines were published before 2022, is there any new work in 2022, like CVPR 2022?

[1] Feature Pyramid Networks for Object Detection

[2] Multi-scale and Cross-scale Contrastive Learning for Semantic Segmentation
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-written and clear. The quality is good. The idea of constructing montage images is novel. Since the method is straightforward and simple, it is not hard to reproduce the model.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the idea of constructing montage images is novel, it also has several limitations as discussed in weakness. The performance improvement is not significant.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The article studies self-supervised dense representation learning. It introduces a multi-level contrastive loss that aims to learn scale-consistent representation from montage assembled images. The method is validated in ImageNet or COCO pre-training, as well as diverse downstream tasks. The results look promising.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

* The paper is well written, and easy to understand.
* Some of the results look good. 

Weaknesses:

* __Motivation:__ The article reveals the weaknesses of some algorithms when pre-training over COCO, and empirically confirms the advantage of the proposed algorithm. However, the model pre-trained on COCO generally gives worse performance than pre-trained on ImageNet. Considering that the same number of training iterations (i.e., same training cost) is used for training over the two datasets, it seems that pre-training on COCO is not practically significant (at least according to the results in this article), thus the claims are also not rigorous enough. 

* __Montage assembly on COCO:__ Montage assembly has been only validated for ImageNet pre-training. However, since the technique is developed to mimic multi-scale multi-object scenarios, I am concerning whether it will still be effective when pre-training on COCO in which images basically cover multi-object scenes. 

* __Ablation study on COCO:__ Following above concerns, it is not obvious to me why the proposed algorithm performs better on COCO than other algorithms. More discussions on the possible reasons should be provided. 

* __Performance comparison against SoCo:__ A proper positional embedding gives +0.5 gains in both $AP^{bb}$ and $AP^{mk}$. This implies that the proposed method, if dropping PE, will be only comparable or even slightly worse against SoCo in Table 3. In this manner, probably that current gains are from the engineering part, rather than from the main contributions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is fine and it is easy to grasp the main idea of the work. However, the motivation should be further clarified. The effect of montage assembly on COCO needs to be verified.
content.summary_of_the_review: I felt that the paper is indeed a borderline paper, in which the multi-level contrastive loss based on montage assembly is somewhat novel, but the validation is not rigorous and not sufficient to confirm the effectiveness of the loss.

content.title: Multi-Level Contrastive Learning for Dense Prediction Task
content.abstract: In this work, we present Multi-Level Contrastive Learning for Dense Prediction Task (MCL), an efficient self-supervised method to learn region-level feature representation for dense prediction tasks. This approach is motivated by the three key factors in detection: localization, scale consistency and recognition. Considering the above factors, we design a novel pretext task, which explicitly encodes absolute position and scale information simultaneously by assembling multi-scale images in a montage manner to mimic multi-object scenario. Unlike the existing image-level self-supervised methods, our method constructs a multi-level contrastive loss by considering each sub-region of the montage image as a singleton to learn a regional semantic representation for translation and scale consistency, while reducing the pre-training epochs to the same as supervised pre-training. Extensive experiments show that MCL consistently outperforms the recent state-of-the-art methods on various datasets with significant margins. In particular, MCL obtains 42.5 AP^bb and 38.3 AP^mk on COCO with the 1x schedule and surpasses MoCo by 4.0 AP^bb and 3.1 AP^mk, when using Mask R-CNN with an R50-FPN backbone pre-trained with 100 epochs. In addition, we further explore the alignment between pretext task and downstream tasks. We extend our pretext task to supervised pre-training, which achieves a similar performance with self-supervised learning, demonstrating the importance of the alignment between pretext task and downstream tasks.
